I've been experimenting with `deno compile` and `deno bundle` on Deno 2.5.6, and I wanted to report a few issues and suggest a feature.

*First problem:*

When I bundle my application with `deno bundle --minify` and then run `deno compile` on the resulting bundle, the executable is generated with no issues, but when running it I get this kind of errors:

```sh
Uncaught SyntaxError: Identifier 'createRequire' has already been declared
import { createRequire } from "node:module";
```

or

```sh
error: Uncaught (in promise) Error: Dynamic require of "node:crypto" is not supported
    at file:///var/folders/qm/yrw8bkgs1lgf3gpbc9qv89c80000gn/T/deno-compile-aarch64-apple-darwin/app.min.js:1:388
    at file:///var/folders/qm/yrw8bkgs1lgf3gpbc9qv89c80000gn/T/deno-compile-aarch64-apple-darwin/app.min.js:1:931
    at file:///var/folders/qm/yrw8bkgs1lgf3gpbc9qv89c80000gn/T/deno-compile-aarch64-apple-darwin/app.min.js:1:500
    at file:///var/folders/qm/yrw8bkgs1lgf3gpbc9qv89c80000gn/T/deno-compile-aarch64-apple-darwin/app.min.js:416:26129
```

I believe this happens because `deno bundle` inlines my code and keeps imports from npm packages like `puppeteer-core` or `@puppeteer/browsers`, which are Node-only (?). Deno 2.5.6 does not resolve npm/jsr imports correctly inside a bundled file, even if they are in the import map.

*Second problem:*

I tried bundling only my own code using `esbuild` and leaving npm/jsr dependencies external, but `deno compile` fails with:

```sh
TS2307 [ERROR]: Import "puppeteer-core" not a dependency and not in import map
```

This shows that Deno cannot resolve npm/jsr modules inside a bundle correctly, even with an import map. Please correct me if I'm wrong!

*Current workaround:*

Compiling the original TypeScript files directly with `deno compile` works fine. The npm/jsr dependencies are resolved correctly, and the binary runs without errors. Minification is not applied, but the binary works.

*Suggestion:*

It would be very useful if deno compile had a --minify flag that:

- Minifies the compiled JS internally before packaging into the binary.
- Works without breaking npm/jsr imports.
- Avoids the need to run deno bundle --minify separately, which currently causes runtime errors with Node-only dependencies.

This would simplify the workflow for Deno projects using npm/jsr packages, allowing both a functional binary and minified code.

The main goal behind this feature requet would be to reduce the size of the compiled binary, while also making the embedded JavaScript code less readable, which can be helpful for both performance and code protection purposes.

Thank you for considering this feature!

label: feature
title: Support graceful shutdown in watch mode
body:
Currently, there is no way in Deno to perform async cleanup actions in watch mode. In Node.js it is possible to listen for `SIGTERM`:

```ts
import process from 'node:process'

process.addListener('SIGINT', () => {
  console.log('Received SIGINT, exiting...')
  process.exit(130)
})

process.addListener('SIGTERM', () => {
  console.log('Received SIGTERM, exiting...')
  setTimeout(() => {
    process.exit(143)
  }, 1000)
})

await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 10_000))
```

Which behaves like:

```
$ node --watch foo.ts
Restarting 'foo.ts'
Received SIGTERM, exiting...
Waiting for graceful termination...
Gracefully restarted 'foo.ts'
Restarting 'foo.ts'
Received SIGTERM, exiting...
Waiting for graceful termination...
Gracefully restarted 'foo.ts'
^CReceived SIGINT, exiting...
```

It is useful for closing DB connections (https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/25609) and cleaning up things like watchers and FFIs (https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12653, https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/20071#issuecomment-2135466035).

Using `addEventListener('unload', () => {})` doesn't work because, like browsers, it cannot prevent/delay unload (https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12653#issuecomment-974862589, https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12653#issuecomment-975318720; https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/25609#issuecomment-2348320939 doesn't reliably work for similar reasons, `pglite.close()` is async API). Moreover, unload listener is not even called on restart when the main thread is blocked (like if you've a top-level await).

Proposed solution - send a signal (`SIGTERM`) while restarting and respect any signal listeners. This will be consistent with Node.js ([[1]](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/51df7b92bc0ab4f54f309d27f6ac49c7d6a5cbd1/lib/internal/main/watch_mode.js#L121-L138), [[2]](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/51df7b92bc0ab4f54f309d27f6ac49c7d6a5cbd1/lib/internal/main/watch_mode.js#L178-L189)) and, unrelated, but also what nodemon supports ([[3]](https://github.com/remy/nodemon?tab=readme-ov-file#gracefully-reloading-down-your-script), [[4]](https://github.com/remy/nodemon?tab=readme-ov-file#controlling-shutdown-of-your-script)). But it likely will need https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/7590 to be fixed first.

label: feature
title: Add an `--outbase` option to `deno bundle` to place outputs next to their source files
body:
**Summary**

`deno bundle` currently supports `--output` and `--outdir`, but there’s no way to mirror each entry point’s relative path when emitting multiple bundles. I’d like a CLI flag (and matching runtime API option) equivalent to esbuild’s `--outbase`, so that bundled `.js` files can be written next to their original `.ts` files (or into a structured `--outdir` that preserves the input directory layout).

**Why this matters**

* Side-by-side outputs keep import paths and deployment layouts stable in repos that expect `*.js` alongside `*.ts` (static sites, Workers, simple CDN hosting).
* It avoids a flat or re-rooted `outdir` that loses directory structure when bundling many entry points.
* Parity with esbuild (which powers `deno bundle`) reduces cognitive friction and makes it easier to migrate existing build scripts.

**Prior art**

esbuild’s `--outbase` (“Base path used to determine entrypoint output paths, for multiple entrypoints”) is the model to match.

**Proposed CLI**

```bash
# Write bundles next to sources
deno bundle --outdir . --outbase . src/**/*.ts

# Or preserve structure under a dedicated outdir
deno bundle --outdir dist --outbase src src/**/*.ts
```

Behavior: for entry points like `src/pages/home.ts` and `src/utils/math.ts`, emit `dist/pages/home.js` and `dist/utils/math.js` (or `pages/home.js` / `utils/math.js` with `--outdir .`), respecting code-splitting as needed.

**Proposed Runtime API**

Add an `outbase?: string` (or similarly named) option to `Deno.bundle()` alongside `outputDir`/`outputPath`, applying the same path-preservation semantics when there are multiple entry points.

**Current behavior / limitation**

`deno bundle` supports `--output` and `--outdir` but not `--outbase`; multiple inputs end up flattened or re-rooted under the chosen `outdir`, which makes it hard to keep per-directory bundles adjacent to their sources.

**Additional context**

* `deno bundle` was reintroduced in Deno 2.4 and has continued to evolve (e.g., HTML entry points in 2.5), so this feels like a natural usability addition.

Thanks for considering!

label: feature
title: Add interactive task picker: `deno task --interactive`
body:
**Summary**

Today, running `deno task` with no args lists the available tasks, but there’s no built-in way to pick and run one interactively. I’m proposing an `--interactive` (`-i`) flag that opens a simple TUI where you can navigate with ↑/↓ and press Enter to run the selected task. This would improve discoverability and ergonomics in projects with many tasks and in workspaces.

**Current behavior**

* `deno task` prints the available tasks (from the current and ancestor configs) and exits. There is no `--interactive` flag today.
* Existing flags include `--filter`/`--recursive` for workspaces, but nothing for interactive selection.

**Proposed behavior**

* `deno task --interactive` (alias `-i`) launches a full-screen or inline selector that lists tasks.
* Keyboard: ↑/↓ to move, Enter to run, Esc/q to quit.
* Optional type-to-filter (basic substring or fuzzy).
* Each row shows the task name; if present, show the `"description"` field as a subtitle.
* Workspace-aware: respects `--filter` and `--recursive` to limit what’s shown.
* After selection, pass through any extra CLI args, e.g. `deno task -i -- --watch`.
* Non-interactive output remains unchanged; `--interactive` only affects the selection UI.

**Why this helps**

* Faster discovery and execution when a project has many tasks or a monorepo workspace.
* Matches common CLI patterns; for example, the `just` task runner offers an interactive chooser via `--choose`.

**Prior art / alternatives**

* External tools like `fzf` can be scripted to approximate this, but a first-party `--interactive` mode would be cross-platform and require no extra dependencies.

**Open questions**

* Should filtering be fuzzy or plain substring?
* Do we show tasks from ancestor `deno.json` files by default (as `deno task` does today), or limit to the nearest config unless `--recursive`/`--filter` is provided?
* Should there be a `DENO_TASK_INTERACTIVE=1` env toggle for users who always want this mode?

title: Security: sandbox FFI (foreign function interface) for code run via --allow-ffi
body:
### Problem

Per the docs: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/ffi/

> [!NOTE]
> **Important security warning:** Unlike JavaScript code running in the Deno sandbox, native libraries loaded via FFI have the same access level as the Deno process itself. This means they can:
> 
> - Access the filesystem
> - Make network connections
> - Access environment variables
> - Execute system commands
> - Always ensure you trust the native libraries you're loading through FFI.

A lot of code relies on `--allow-ffi`, like database-related libraries.

The use of `--allow-ffi` essentially nullifies Deno's sandbox.

### Solution

Create a sandbox to sandbox native-code libraries, and tie it in to the same sandboxing permissions that Deno uses with JavaScript.

Potentially useful projects:

- https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap

label: feature
title: Add support for compression dictionary transport
body:
[Compression dictionary transport](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-compression-dictionary/) is a HTTP mechanism for negotiating and using compression dictionaries for brotli and zstd-based content encodings. Depending on the use case, it can result in 90%+ smaller payloads than brotli or zstd alone.

It is also being defined in terms of fetch: https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/pull/1854

For deno there are two interesting use cases:
1 - As defined in the spec where a dictionary is configured through the Use-As-Dictionary response header and used transparently for future requests.
2 - Applications may find it useful to explicitly configure a dictionary (that ships with the binary for example) to be used with a given fetch request. In this case, the same `Available-Dictionary` and `Accept-Encoding` can be used but it doesn't require that the dictionary be provided over the network.

label: feature
title: Enabling/Disabling Opentelemetry during runtime
body:
Currently, OpenTelemetry configuration in Deno appears to be set at startup and cannot be modified during runtime. This limitation prevents applications from dynamically enabling or disabling telemetry based on runtime conditions such as:

- Performance considerations during high-load periods
- Debug modes that need to be toggled without restarting the application
- Feature flags or A/B testing scenarios

### Expected Behavior
Deno should provide APIs to:
- Enable OpenTelemetry tracing/metrics collection during runtime
- Disable OpenTelemetry collection to reduce overhead when not needed
- Modify telemetry configuration (sampling rates, exporters, etc.) without restart

### Use Cases
- Dynamic Configuration: Applications that pull configuration from remote sources need to adjust telemetry settings without downtime
- Performance Optimization: Ability to disable telemetry during peak traffic to reduce overhead
- Development/Debug Workflows: Toggle detailed tracing on/off for troubleshooting specific issues
- Cost Management: Dynamically adjust sampling rates based on operational needs

### Proposed Solution
Consider exposing runtime APIs similar to other OpenTelemetry implementations that allow:

`Deno.telemetry.enable()`
`Deno.telemetry.disable()`
`Deno.telemetry.configure(options)`

label: docs
title: Possible discrepancy in Deno CLI default for `--allow-import`: `user.githubusercontent.com` vs. documented `gist.githubusercontent.com`
body:
Version: Deno v2.5.3

When examining the default allowed hosts for the `--allow-import` permission, I've found a discrepancy between the Deno ~~v2.4.0~~v2.0.0 through v2.5.3 documentation and the output of the `deno run --help` command.

Permission options:
Docs: https://docs.deno.com/go/permissions

The documentation currently states:
> By default Deno allows importing sources from following hosts:
> deno.land
> esm.sh
> jsr.io
> cdn.jsdelivr.net
> raw.githubusercontent.com
> gist.githubusercontent.com

However, the output of `deno run --help` for `--allow-import` shows:
```
  -I, --allow-import[=<IP_OR_HOSTNAME>...] Allow importing from remote hosts. Optionally specify allowed IP addresses and host names, with ports as necessary.
                                            Default value: deno.land:443,jsr.io:443,esm.sh:443,cdn.jsdelivr.net:443,raw.githubusercontent.com:443,user.githubusercontent.com:443
                                             --allow-import  |  --allow-import="example.com,github.com"
```

The key difference is that the documentation lists `gist.githubusercontent.com`, while `deno run --help` lists `user.githubusercontent.com`.

**Question:**

Which host is the correct default for `--allow-import` permissions: `user.githubusercontent.com:443` or `gist.githubusercontent.com:443`?

**Context:**

This discrepancy was observed in Deno ~~v2.4.0~~v2.0.0 (and later versions, including 2.5.3). I noticed this when comparing the Deno documentation with the actual help output.

Looking at the codebase for Deno v2.5.3, the `flags.rs` file includes `user.githubusercontent.com`:
* [https://github.com/denoland/deno/blob/v2.5.3/cli/args/flags.rs#L4326](https://github.com/denoland/deno/blob/v2.5.3/cli/args/flags.rs#L4326) (across 2 lines)

And the `_commands_reference.json` file also includes `user.githubusercontent.com`:
* [https://github.com/denoland/docs/blob/3006b6ed924a04ed57dfdbfd750d4fd3a4955337/runtime/reference/cli/_commands_reference.json#L1955](https://github.com/denoland/docs/blob/3006b6ed924a04ed57dfdbfd750d4fd3a4955337/runtime/reference/cli/_commands_reference.json#L1955) (across 6 lines)

This suggests an inconsistency between the implemented default and the documented default. Clarification is needed on which is the intended and currently active default for `--allow-import`.

title: `deno doc` assigns doc with `@module` tag to multiple symbols
body:
Version: Deno 2.5.1 (reproes since 1.0.0)

### Description

A module doc tagged with `@module` is assigned to both the module and the first symbol in the file if the first symbol is undocumented. Expecting the first symbol to be left undocumented.

### Example (bug.js)

```js
/**
 * This is the module doc.
 *
 * @module
 */

export function foo() {}

/** This is the bar function. */
export function bar() {}
```

### `deno doc` behavior

```sh
deno doc bug.js
```
```
Defined in file:///workspaces/deno-bug/bug.js:1:1

  This is the module doc.

  @module

Defined in file:///workspaces/deno-bug/bug.js:10:1

function bar(): void
  This is the bar function.

Defined in file:///workspaces/deno-bug/bug.js:7:1

function foo(): void
  This is the module doc.

  @module

```

`deno doc --lint` should fail, but it does not:

```sh
deno doc --lint bug.js
```
```
Checked 1 file
```

### `jsdoc` behavior

```sh
jsdoc --version
```
```
JSDoc 4.0.4 (Sat, 19 Oct 2024 19:05:34 GMT)
```
```sh
jsdoc --explain bug.js | jq '.[] | select(.description != null) | {name,kind,description}'
```
```json
{
  "name": "bug",
  "kind": "module",
  "description": "This is the module doc."
}
{
  "name": "bar",
  "kind": "function",
  "description": "This is the bar function."
}
```

title: Must wait for `Deno.Listener.accept` to reject after calling `Deno.Listener.close`
body:
I've just discovered that after a call to `Deno.Listener.close`, if I attempt to call `Deno.listen` on the same port, I get `AddrInUse` error, and the best way I found to avoid this is to wait for any `Deno.Listener.accept` calls (or `Deno.Listener[Symbol.asyncIterator]`).

<details>
<summary>Example server code</summary>

```typescript
const server = Deno.listen({ port: 10000 });
server.accept().catch(() => {});
server.close();
Deno.listen({ port: 10000 }); //< AddrInUse
```
</details>

The only information I managed to find was on `Deno.Listener.close` which said 
>Any pending accept promises will be rejected with errors.

With the lack of documentation on the functions in question, I'm not able to determine if this is desired behaviour or not, so I've assumed it is. 

Is it possible to either:
* Change `Deno.Listener.close` to actually close the socket
* Change `Deno.listen` to wait for sockets that have been requested to close before opening
* Add/change documentation to explain this requirement, on one or more of these functions

label: docs
title: Consider moving manual/docs to a separate repo
body:
https://deno.land/manual is the "source for truth" and main documentation for Deno. 

These docs are generated from files in [`docs/`](https://github.com/denoland/deno/tree/main/docs) directory.

I don't have a data to back it up, but it is my impression that going through full Deno CI is discouraging contributions to manual; after all there are several pages on how to contribute to the repo and setting up dev environment is non-trivial. Additionally CI can take anywhere from 20 to 40 minutes.

Hereby I propose to move `docs/` directory to a separate repository (`deno_manual`) with its own CI. 

Here are pros and cons for this proposal.

Pros:
- contributing will be significantly easier as the only requirement would be to have `deno` installed on your system (to run `deno fmt`)
- CI will take less than 1 minute (quick development loop)
- we could even enable auto-formatting in CI, so the PRs that are opened via "Edit" button in Github wouldn't fails more often than not

Cons:
- another repo to maintain (would need to tag and release in unison with Deno release); although the maintenance cost should be marginal

All in all, I believe moving documentation to a separate repo will have a positive effect on the state of the manual as it would be trivial to contribute to it, which hasn't been the case lately in main repo.

Kinda off-topic but https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/11170 would immensely help to keep manual up to date by type-checking examples in codeblock (we already have this functionality for JSDocs, the issue is about adding ability to typecheck codeblock in markdown files).

label: docs
title: Closer should return a Promise
body:
Deno `Conn`s provide a `Reader`, `Writer`, and `Closer`. The first two are promise driven apis, the last one is not.

There are possibly many async operations (one trying to read, and many other async writes) in an active connection.
When calling `close()` on the connection, it is possible that there are many pending writer ops, enough that any simple test reading/writing will fail with resource leakage (thanks for this).

This means that in order to close in a somewhat clean way, all API clients will have to set up a promise that resolves on a read failure (similar issue on `listen`) and track the individual promises returned by write into a stack and `shift()` them out as they resolve.

The setup to call `close()` typically means setting up a flag to ignore any read/write attempts from some other async operation trying to use the connection, and then waiting on the reader promise and all the write promises to resolve/fail. Only then can `close()` be called.

Since the `Conn` should know about the state of the read and the number of pending writes scheduled, it seems reasonable to prevent much of this boilerplate by simply returning a promise from close(), which would signal at that point when the controlling process can safely exit or whatnot.

label: question
title: No way to opt out of global Node.js types (since 2.8.0)
body:
## Summary

Since v2.8.0, Deno includes the Node.js type lib globally by default, and there doesn't seem to be a way to opt out.

## Reproduction

```ts
const _timeout: number = setTimeout(() => {});
```

On Deno 2.8.0 or higher (currently 2.9.1), this fails with:

```
Type 'Timeout' is not assignable to type 'number'.
```

On 2.7.14 and earlier, it type-checks fine. `setTimeout` returning `number` matches the browser behavior.

## Background

I originally started writing this as a bug report. I assumed some package was importing the Node.js types and Deno was failing to exclude them. While isolating the issue, I realized the change was intentional:

> feat: include node lib by default and use NodeJS.Timeout for timers (#33823)

The node lib is pulled in via a `/// <reference lib="node" />` directive inside `lib.deno.shared_globals.d.ts`, so every Deno lib includes it. Setting `compilerOptions.lib` doesn't help, since you can't get Deno's globals without the Node.js types coming along.

I just realized this today after upgrading the Deno version of an old project, seeing Node.js type errors inside Deno truly feels like a bug. I was surprised how such an obvious bug could live until 2.9.1.

Turns out it was intentional. I have no idea why while there is `@types/node`.

## Why this matters

One of Deno's core promises (selling point) has always been browser API compatibility: web-standard APIs behaving the way they do in the browser. In the browser, `setTimeout` returns a `number`, and code written against web standards expects that. With this change, web-compatible code now type-errors under Deno, while Node-specific patterns are the ones that type-check.

Node.js compat is valuable, and I understand wanting `NodeJS.Timeout` patterns to work for people porting legacy code. But making the Node.js types global for everyone inverts the default: projects that don't touch `node:` at all (some on purpose) still get Node's type environment. Those who need it could opt in (as they already can with `@types/node`), rather than everyone else having no way to opt out.

## Expected

Either make the node lib opt-in, or at minimum provide a way to exclude it while keeping the Deno globals, so web-standard code can keep type-checking as it does in the browser.

If there will be a Node.js compat layer, that should be hidden from the user and should only apply to external packages until its not needed anymore.

title: Why does `deno run` use the network without the `--allow-net` flag (or including the --deny-net flag)
body:
I'm in the process of switching away from Node as much as possible, and came across a change to not use npx in favour of Deno.

```
deno run npm:wrangler pages blah blah
```

Per the docs: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/node/

```
# deno run allows remote execution of a package from various locations,
# and can scoped to npm via the `npm:` specifier.
$ deno run -A npm:create-next-app@latest
```

This is the error after blocking the network connection:

```
error: Failed loading https://registry.npmjs.org/wrangler for package "wrangler"

Caused by:
    error sending request for url (https://registry.npmjs.org/wrangler): client error (Connect): tcp connect error: Bad file descriptor (os error 9)
```

npmjs isn't on the list of allowed URLS: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/#network-access


Now, I think the nuance here is that the docs specifically state "executing code"?
```
executing code can not make network requests, open network listeners or perform DNS resolution. This includes making HTTP requests, opening TCP/UDP sockets, and listening for incoming connections on TCP or UDP.
```

So, I'm guessing that the intention is that Deno itself can have all permissions, but just the thing that Deno is running can't? I have to admit, I was a bit surprised to see my network blocker pop up when running that command.

- Cache all dependencies and then run the `demo compile` command with the `--cached-only` flag. Same result.

label: question
title: deno compile ignores -o <name> when compilation is run from outside the project root (input file is not in the cwd)
body:
Version: Deno 2.3.6

### Reproduction Steps

1. Create a directory and initialize a Deno project:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/work/foo
cd ~/work/foo
deno init
cd ..
```

2. From outside the project root (`~/work`), run:

```bash
deno compile foo/main.ts -o out.bin
```

---

### Observed Behavior

```bash
~/work ❯ deno compile foo/main.ts -o out.bin
Check file:///home/user/work/foo/main.ts
Compile file:///home/user/work/foo/main.ts to foo
error: Could not compile to file 'foo' because a directory exists with the same name. You can use the `--output <file-path>` flag to provide an alternative name.
```

Despite explicitly using the `-o out.bin` argument, Deno:

- Logs that it's compiling "to foo"
- Attempts to emit the binary as `foo` rather than `out.bin`
- Fails if a `foo/` directory exists which should be irrelevant unless the `-o` was set to the same name

Additionally, if the compile command is run from any directory other than the project's direct parent like:

```bash
cd /tmp
deno compile ~/work/foo/main.ts -o out.bin
```

Deno still ignores the `-o` flag and instead emits a binary named `foo` directly into the current directory (i.e. `/tmp/foo`), not `out.bin`.

---

### Expected Behavior

- The compiler must respect the `--output` flag without referencing the source path or its parent directory.
- The output path specified via `-o` should always be used literally and without fallback logic.
- Compilation should succeed regardless of the current working directory or source location, as long as the `-o` path is valid and doesn't match any existing path.

---

### Additional Context

This appears to be a long-standing issue. A similar issue was previously raised in [#12759](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/12759) but closed without being resolved, it only suggests using `--output` which appears to be broken as I stated above.

This bug creates serious friction in CI scripts, project automation, and build tools that rely on predictable output behavior.

title: Implement `npm explain` subcommand
body:
I've found myself sometimes wondering why I particular nested dependency ends up in `deno.lock`. With npm there is the [explain](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v7/commands/npm-explain) subcommand, which shows the dependents of a particular subdependency. [why](https://yarnpkg.com/cli/why) is the yarn equivalent, and pnpm also appears to have a similar [why](https://pnpm.io/cli/why) subcommand.

The current deno subcommands for dependency management are great. I hope that deno can implement a subcommand to make it easier to traverse the dependency tree backwards, i.e. recursively finding the packages that depend on a particular package.

title: support compiling a local npm package
body:
If I have a local npm project, I expect to do something like this.

```
cd my-project
npm pack
deno compile -o my-project-binary file:my-project-0.0.1.tgz
./my-project-binary
```

PS. This is kind of similar to being able to execute

```
npm install -g my-project-0.0.1.tgz
```

## context

I am trying to compile an npm project using `deno compile` for GitHub release assets. My current approach is to publish to `npm` and wait until it's published, and then use `deno compile` with the npm specifier and the latest version tag.

If this support lands on `deno`, I don't have to wait for `npm publish`.

## tried solution

I tried manually extracting the tar to `node_modules/` and `node_modules/.deno`. It works with `--node-modules-dir=manual`. That is, I can successfully execute

$ deno run --node-modules-dir=manual npm:my-project

error: Resolving npm specifier entrypoints this way is currently not supported with "nodeModules": "manual". In the meantime, try with --node-modules-dir=auto instead

If I set `--node-modules-dir=auto`, `deno` tries to pull the npm registry data -- but my project is not published on npm.

deno test -A --parallel --clean --coverage --trace-leaks

Also, the error suggests that it must be an unawaited call to async FS API, which is not the case.

The error report is consistent across failures, meaning the same file/module, the same `const [...] = await Deno.readTextFile([...])` call.

Also should note that this failure is the only failure in the step that runs deno and there's no other test failures.

These started when we added tests for some functions that use temp files as buffers. We can't tell from which version of Deno this could have started, but the first time we got them we were already on version 2.0.x.

Also, these started without the `--trace-leaks` param, and the behavior has not changed since introducing `--trace-leaks`.

Have never been able to repro it on macos, though.

label: question
title: How to scale OTEL instrumentation in Deno without opinionated defaults?
body: Hi everyone, especially @lucacasonato I'm currently integrating OpenTelemetry (OTEL) in Deno and have a question regarding the current approach. From my perspective, I’m struggling to understand how this implementation is meant to scale in the long run. It seems that there are no opinionated defaults, leaving it entirely up to the developer to define and manage everything manually. When a trace is started, I can modify the name and add values globally on the middleware level. However, when Deno makes sub-requests within that trace, these do not automatically inherit meaningful names or status information—they remain undefined unless explicitly set by the developer. This makes me wonder how one is supposed to scale instrumentation properly—would I need to manually update every single sub-request span myself? Or is this actually the intended way to use OTEL in Deno? Personally, I think it would make sense to provide at least some opinionated defaults, such as setting the span name to something like METHOD /pathname. Since Deno already tracks sub-requests, why not also set the status and a reasonable default name automatically? These pieces of information should already be available, so it feels like an unnecessary burden to require developers to handle them manually. Since I’m a newbie when it comes to OTEL, I’d really appreciate some clarification. Thanks in advance! 😊

label: question
title: Add lint rule for missing import file extension
body:
Some projects use Deno as the runtime and linter, but not as the LSP (e.g. Next JS). In these projects, if you import a file without specifying the file extension (`.js`/`.ts`), the Typescript LSP will just accept it. But then there is no way to catch these oversights. If there was a `deno lint` rule that checked for this, that would help in projects like that.

Note: this is only relevant, because the Deno LSP is not yet suitable for use with certain projects (e.g. Next JS). If it was possible to use it for those types of projects, this rule might be unnecessary, because the LSP would catch the missing extensions anyways.

body:
$ deno --version
deno 2.1.8 (stable, release, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
v8 13.0.245.12-rusty
typescript 5.6.2

I have the following code:

```js
for (const h of expandGlobSync('**')) {
	console.dir(h)
}
```
which prints out the following (truncated):

```text
{
  path: "C:\\Users\\johnd\\utils\\test\\llutils\\file2.txt",
  name: "file2.txt",
  isFile: true,
  isDirectory: false,
  isSymlink: false
}
{
  path: "C:\\Users\\johnd\\utils\\test\\llutils\\file3.flags.txt",
  name: "file3.flags.txt",
  isFile: true,
  isDirectory: false,
  isSymlink: false
}
```
Note that this is JS code - there's no type checking being done.
The objects being printed are of type WalkEntry. However, the documentation for WalkEntry only lists the 'path' key as existing an a WalkEntry.

That may just sound like a bug in the documentation, but here is my situation. I'm using a language called civet, which is CoffeeScript-like, but handles TypeScript syntax. Consider the following civet code:

```coffee
import {expandGlobSync} from '@std/fs/expand-glob'
for (const h of expandGlobSync('**/*.txt')) {
	console.log(h.isFile);
	}
```

When I attempt to type check this file, using the command `civet --typecheck temp.civet`, I get the following error:

```text 
test/temp.civet.tsx:3:16 - error TS2339: Property 'isFile' does not exist on type 'WalkEntry'.

3  console.log(h.isFile);
                 ~~~~~~
```

I'm certainly not asking for you to support civet, but I can't help believing that you're doing something pretty funky with the WalkEntry type definition for civet to not realize that it includes the keys isFile, isDirectory, isSynlink, and probably name also. Somehow, though, it seems that Deno realizes that those fields are there.

title: `--import-map` option seems inconsistent from `imports` or `importMap` field in `deno.json`
body:
Version: Deno 2.1.4

It appears that the `--import-map` option handles sub-paths differently compared
to the `imports` or `importMap` fields in `deno.json`. Below are the test code
and import map used for this observation.

##### **test.ts**

```typescript
import { delay } from "@std/async/delay";

console.log("Waiting for 1 second...");
await delay(1000);
console.log("Done!");
```

##### **import_map.json**

```json
{
  "imports": {
    "@std/async": "jsr:@std/async@^1.0.0"
  }
}
```

When `import_map.json` is referenced via the `importMap` field in `deno.json`
(or written directly within `deno.json`), the script works as expected:

```bash
$ deno run test.ts
Waiting for 1 second...
Done!
```

However, when using the `--import-map` option instead, an error occurs
indicating that `@std/async/delay` is not included in the import map:

```bash
$ deno run --no-config --import-map import_map.json test.ts
error: Relative import path "@std/async/delay" not prefixed with / or ./ or ../ and not in import map from "file:///Users/alisue/ogh/lambdalisue/deno-import-map-issue/test.ts"
    at file:///Users/alisue/ogh/lambdalisue/deno-import-map-issue/test.ts:1:23
```

This issue seems to be related to the concept of
[Packages via Trailing Slashes](https://github.com/WICG/import-maps?tab=readme-ov-file#packages-via-trailing-slashes)
as described in the import maps README. However, the resolution of specifiers
appears to fail when using the `--import-map` option.

##### **import_map_trailing.json**

```json
{
  "imports": {
    "@std/async": "jsr:@std/async@^1.0.0",
    "@std/async/": "jsr:@std/async@^1.0.0/"
  }
}
```

Using this import map still results in an error:

```bash
$ deno run --no-config --import-map import_map_trailing.json test.ts
error: Failed to resolve the specifier "@std/async/delay" as its after-prefix portion "delay" could not be URL-parsed relative to the URL prefix "jsr:@std/async@^1.0.0/" mapped to by the prefix "@std/async/"
    at file:///Users/alisue/ogh/lambdalisue/deno-import-map-issue/test.ts:1:23
```

To resolve this issue, specifying the full path in the import map works as a
workaround:

##### **import_map_workaround.json**

```json
{
  "imports": {
    "@std/async": "jsr:@std/async@^1.0.0",
    "@std/async/delay": "jsr:@std/async@^1.0.0/delay"
  }
}
```

With this import map, the script executes correctly:

```bash
$ deno run --no-config --import-map import_map_workaround.json test.ts
Waiting for 1 second...
Done!
```

label: question
title: Add support for multiple import maps
body:
Import maps currently have to load before any ES module and there can only be a single import map per document. That makes them fragile and potentially slow to use in real-life scenarios: Any module that loads before them breaks the entire app, and in apps with many modules the become a large blocking resource, as the entire map for all possible modules needs to load first.

There's an HTML PR [proposal](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10528) to enable multiple import maps per document, by merging them in a consistent and deterministic way.

I'd appreciate y'all's opinions.
